display.title: The Alter Rebbe the Firefighter and the Baal Shem Tov's Mirror
display.summary_short: Why Rosh Hashanah is the 'head' of the year and why we daven every day, then the Alter Rebbe stops a town fire and a general tells of the Baal Shem Tov's wondrous mirror.
display.summary_long: The storyteller opens with the Mitteler Rebbe's question: why is Rosh Hashanah called the 'head' of the year? Like the brain directing the body, everything we receive all year is decided then. So why daven every day? Chassidus compares it to a bank account: Hashem deposits the year's brachos on Rosh Hashanah, and daily davening withdraws them, like a king who gives his son money for only a month so he will keep visiting. He then explains why we must not interrupt from Baruch She'amar until after Shemoneh Esrei, comparing it to a blocked water pipe. The story: the Alter Rebbe, who called the Baal Shem Tov his 'Zeide', is visiting a town of wooden houses when a fire spreads beyond the firemen and soldiers. He stands leaning on his cane and stares at the flames until they die down. The impressed general invites him and reads from his father's diary: the Baal Shem Tov once showed his worried father, through a mirror, his wife writing a letter home announcing the birth of a son, the general himself. The Alter Rebbe blesses the general to treat Jews kindly.
display.lesson: Everything for the year is set on Rosh Hashanah, and daily davening brings those brachos down, so daven with attention and without interruption. A tzaddik's power comes from Hashem and from his connection to his Rebbeim.

advisories.note: A fire threatens a whole town; a general threatens to quarter soldiers in Jewish homes. Resolved without harm.
